pages.x: Around 559 BC Cyrus became king of Anshan, a small Persian kingdom in the south of Iran, under the rule of the Medes. Legend said that his grandfather, the Median king Astyages, had dreamed that the boy would take his throne, and ordered him killed as a baby, but a herdsman raised him instead.

Around 553 BC Cyrus rose against Astyages. When Astyages marched into Persia, part of his army mutinied under a noble, Harpagus, and handed the king over. Cyrus took the Median capital, Ecbatana, and its treasure, and the Persians became masters of the Medes' empire, from the Zagros to central Anatolia.

Croesus of Lydia, the richest king of his day, decided to strike first, after the oracle at Delphi told him that if he attacked he would destroy a great empire. He did: his own. Cyrus followed him home to Sardis, frightened his horses with camels, whose smell they could not stand, and took the citadel.

Herodotus tells that Cyrus set the captured Croesus on a pyre to be burned, and that Croesus called out the name of Solon, the Athenian wise man who had told him that no one can be called happy until he is dead. Moved, Cyrus ordered the fire put out, and a sudden storm of rain did it for him.

In 539 BC Cyrus turned on Babylon, the greatest city in the world. Its king, Nabonidus, had angered the priests of the city's god, Marduk. Cyrus beat his army at Opis, and his general entered Babylon without a fight. A clay cylinder later told how Cyrus had come as a peacemaker, chosen by Marduk himself.

Cyrus let the peoples whom the Babylonians had deported go home. Among them were the Jews, exiled since Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem, and many returned to rebuild the Temple. The Bible calls Cyrus the anointed of the Lord, the only foreign king it honours so.

Cyrus spent his last years on the steppe frontier. Herodotus says that in 530 BC he was killed fighting the Massagetae, nomads east of the Caspian, and that their queen, Tomyris, whose son had died through his trickery, had his head plunged into a skin full of blood, so that he could drink his fill.

His son Cambyses II took on the last great power of the Near East. With water supplied by Arab chiefs he crossed Sinai, and in 525 BC crushed the army of the young pharaoh Psamtik III at Pelusium, then took Memphis. A later tale says his soldiers carried cats, sacred to the Egyptians, in front of them.

The Persians now ruled from the Aegean to Central Asia and the Nile, the largest empire the world had yet seen. Cyrus was remembered, even by the Greeks who fought his heirs, as the model of a wise and tolerant king, and his tomb still stands at Pasargadae, in Iran.
pts: Cyrus beat the Medes, Lydia and Babylon
